author: Joe Schroeder
title: '100% success': Raw sewage is now unlikely to flow into White River, according to Carmel officials - NewsBreak
text:
By Joe Schroeder ,
9 hours ago
CARMEL, Ind. — Officials with the city of Carmel say they have flipped the script on whether or not a wastewater main will break and leak raw sewage into the White River. This comes after historic severe weather and flooding swept through the area.
Flipping the odds Carmel Engineering Director Bradley Pease said on Monday that there was an 85-90% chance that the city's main sanitary pipe would burst due to an unprecedented amount of flooding in the area.
In an update on Wednesday afternoon, Pease said that the odds have flipped and that there is now only a 10% chance of the wastewater main failing.
How Hoosiers impacted by severe weather, flooding can receive assistance Carmel Mayor Sue Finkam said that, thanks to the help of many local and state agencies, the city is now in a "much better position."
This is due to the quick construction of two temporary dams near the area of Blue Woods Creek.
"A beautiful dam" By using two Black Hawk helicopters, the Indiana National Guard was able to come in overnight and place 73 bags of sand weighing 2,000 pounds each along the creek bed.
The other dam was built near the Martin Marietta quarry and constructed with more than 150 truckloads of concrete that were brought in to stabilize the bank. Pease called the operation a "100% success," adding that the National Guard built a "beautiful dam."
"We got a chance to do our jobs," said Lt. Col. Ben Ramos. "It looks and appears to be a success."
Bridge collapse updates Hamilton County Commissioner Christine Altman also spoke Wednesday and gave updates on the collapse of the Hazel Dell Parkway bridge, which is considered Carmel's biggest infrastructure loss.
Altman confirmed on Monday that the bridge will need a "total replacement" and is being considered a complete loss.
An overhead view of the Hazel Dell Parkway bridge (WXIN/WTTV) On Wednesday, Altman said the county has hired United Consulting to help work on the bridge redesign. Officials are now also working with the Indiana Department of Environmental Management, the Army Corps of Engineers and the Indiana Department of Natural Resources.
Officials have reportedly "devised a plan" to get rid of the debris expected to fill the water. After cleanup, they will soon host a bid for contractors to potentially rebuild the bridge.
How to help those affected by Indiana’s historic flooding Altman did say that commissioners "explored a solution" that involved reopening the bridge with two lanes, but said that it was both "cost-prohibitive" and would cause significant delays in fixing the bridge.
She added that they are "close to having a contract to sign" that would organize the disposal of damage, and that they are looking to ask the Federal Emergency Management Agency for damage reimbursement.
Moving forward Finkam said that, of the 215 homes affected by power outages during the flooding, 41 remain without power. For immediate assistance or advice on how to re-enter a home after flooding, Carmel Fire officials suggested calling Indiana 211 and “exercising extreme caution.”
In a news release sent Monday evening, the Hamilton County Assessor’s Office said that homeowners whose properties were “significantly damaged” by flooding may be eligible for property tax relief.
“We know many property owners are dealing with significant damage, and we want to make sure they understand what options may be available to them,” says Hamilton County Assessor Kevin Poore. “Each property will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis, so we encourage anyone who believes they may qualify to contact our office with questions and submit the required form.”
Homeowners looking to qualify must complete State Form 137R and submit it to the Assessor’s Office no later than Dec. 31, 2027. For more information, call the Assessor’s Office at (317) 776-9617.
